references.text: Matthew's parallel account of the transfiguration on the mountain, where Jesus takes Peter, James, and John up a high mountain. Matthew specifies 'six days later' instead of Luke's 'about eight days'.
Mark's parallel account of the transfiguration on the mountain, where Jesus takes Peter, James, and John up a high mountain. Mark also specifies 'six days later', as in Matthew.

The preceding context in Luke, where Jesus asks his disciples who people say he is, Peter's confession, and Jesus' prediction of his suffering – the words ('τοὺς λόγους τούτους') to which verse 28 refers back.
Another occasion when Jesus chose specifically Peter, John, and James as his closest disciples – at the raising of Jairus' daughter.
Also in Gethsemane, Jesus takes Peter, James, and John with him, showing that these three formed an inner circle among the twelve.
Jesus went up on the mountain to pray, just as he does here. Luke places special emphasis on Jesus' prayer life, and this is another example of Jesus withdrawing to the mountain to pray.
Jesus goes to the Mount of Olives to pray, again with his disciples. Luke once more highlights the connection between mountains, prayer, and revelation.
Peter refers back to the transfiguration on the mountain as an eyewitness account of Jesus' majesty, specifically mentioning the holy mountain where they were with him.
Moses took Aaron, Nadab, and Abihu up Mount Sinai to meet God – a typological parallel to Jesus taking three disciples up the mountain for divine revelation.
Moses' face shone when he came down from Mount Sinai after speaking with God, an Old Testament parallel to Jesus' transfiguration on the mountain.
